articles.text: The 19th Annual Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast will take place this Sunday, September 8, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 noon at Beach Elementary School, 100 Lake Avenue. As with every year, hundreds of community members will enjoy plates of buttermilk, blueberry, chocolate chip or oatmeal pancakes, plus sausage, bacon, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee. A student jazz band will serenade breakfast-goers as they eat. The cost is $15 for adults and $10 for kids and seniors. Tickets will be sold on-site, and no pre-registration is needed. All proceeds will benefit the Beach Parents Organization (BPO) which provides funding assistance for Beach Elementary School’s educational programs and sponsors after-school enrichment classes. “I want to go all in and help the community as much as I can with this fundraiser,” said Michael Wilhelm, president of the Beach Dads Club, a position known affectionately to the other club members as “Padre Grande.” Wilhelm took over the role from the previous president, Michael Gross, at the Beach Dads’ Welcome Night on August 21. Funds raised will go toward classroom materials, library support, STEM resources, science materials, lunchtime activities, assemblies, speakers, musical instruments, art and library supplies, and teacher and staff appreciation activities. articles.text: The parent-run Piedmont School District Wellness Center is hosting a pickleball tournament titled Positively Pickled on Saturday, September 21, with three divisions of play (beginner, intermediate and competitive). After a five-minute warmup each team will play three matches against similar teams. Team registration is $100. Last school year, the Wellness Center provided over 2,000 therapy sessions to Piedmont students; this fundraising effort helps ensure that Piedmont students continue to receive the mental health support they need. The Wellness Center delivers free counseling and mental health services to Piedmont High School, Middle School, and Millennium High School students. The center helps students manage emotional and social challenges, including stress, depression, grief, relationship conflicts, and substance use concerns. articles.text: The 23rd annual Chalk Art Festival will return to the Beach School playground this Sunday, September 8, between 9 a.m. and Noon. The school’s blacktop will be divided into roughly 100 squares that parents can purchase for their child to draw on with boxes of brightly colored pastel chalk provided by Flax Art & Design. Individual squares are available for $20 each at the time of the event. All proceeds will benefit the Piedmont Arts Fund, a part of the Piedmont Education Foundation that supports art in Piedmont schools. “It’s a great community event,” said Jon Schleuning, who organizes the Chalk Art Festival. “Every year, the blacktop literally transforms into this amazing kaleidoscope explosion of color.” Three artists pay homage to the Pixar film Elemental with chalk art in 2023. Founded in 2002, by Havens school art teachers Raul Jorcino and Karen Stanton, the Chalk Art Festival has become a well-loved tradition among Piedmont families. “People come back year after year for generations. It has A pair of girls work on their chalk square in 2023. become this event where people, parents and their kids habitually come back and do their squares together each year,” said Schleuning. Schleuning added that he believes that the opportunity for kids to express themselves artistically is what keeps people coming back. “You literally start with a blank square and you have permission to do pretty much anything you want,” he explained. Subject matter for artists’ chalk squares in the past has ranged from pancakes and rainbows to spooky graveyards and Halloween costumes. The Chalk Art Festival is held in conjunction with the Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast. Both are hosted at the same time at Beach School. For more information about the Piedmont Arts Fund, visit their website at www.piedmontartsfund.org. A girl focuses on blending colors together with a paintbrush. A young artist draws a pastel rainbow.

articles.text: Introducing one-year-old Chihuahua mix Tater Tot. This 13-pound affectionate cutie is available for adoption or foster. Oakland Animal Services staff and volunteers say Tater Tot can be a bit shy when meeting new people, but once he knows someone he loves to sit in laps and cuddle. He enjoys playing with other small dogs and would do well in a home with a playful doggie sibling to show him the ropes. Tater Tot has had a chance to go on a couple of outings where he demonstrated good progress in leash walking skills and was not reactive to other dogs, bicycles or people. On a trip to Tilden Park, Tater Tot easily hiked 3+ miles in the company of a volunteer and a 10-year-old child. At an ice cream stop, he sat contentedly on a bench next to the volunteer and accepted pets, patiently waiting and not begging while they ate their snack. He was an ideal al fresco dining companion! Tater Tot, a Chihuahua mix, at Oakland Animal Services. If you would like to foster Tater Tot email dogfostering@ oaklandsanimals.org. If you would like to adopt him, come meet him Thursday from 12 - 7 pm, or Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Tater Tot must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. articles.text: Camp Augusta will host its annual Wish, Wonder & Wine fundraiser on Saturday, September 21 from 5:00-7:00 p.m. in the courtyard at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Tickets are $50 and are available at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/wish-wonderand-wine-tickets-945283286757 ?aff=oddtdtcreator. As school begins, keep an eye out for the cornflower blue shirts around town worn by the hundreds of Piedmont children who attended Camp Augusta this summer. They may not know it, but they are continuing a long tradition in the community. You are invited to learn more about this special place that so many children call home each summer. Join us on September 21st for Wish, Wonder & Wine, an adult evening of fun in Piedmont. Enjoy wine, appetizers, and auction prizes while building community in support of Camp Augusta. You’ll hear from staff and campers with exciting updates from this summer, including the hugely popular new ropes challenge course. Camp offers amazing programming and some of the highest trained camp staff in the world to run the program. Help us meet our goal of upgrading our staff housing and to kick off a two-year capital campaign to replace those structures and the Cedar Bath house. Piedmont History Camp Augusta was originally donated to the girls of Piedmont almost 100 years ago. In the early years, the camp’s main use was by the Piedmont Council of Camp Fire. Virtually all the young Piedmont women spent their summers at the camp. After the site was shuttered by the Camp Fire organization, a group of dedicated Piedmonters formed an oversight board and began the long legal battle to win the property back for the children of Piedmont. While the site sat dormant for decades, the facilities fell into disrepair. However, with hard work and the support of the community, the 90 acre facility located in the beautiful forested foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains has received a variety of improvements over the years: the restoration of the original Lodge where campers hang out in aerial silks; a kitchen where our chefs cook delicious organic food that campers get excited about (have you ever tried Australian pizza with bananas on top!?); and this year’s incredible new high ropes challenge course with over 40 elements to ascend. articles.text: The co-ed “Wild Things” adult softball team won the summer league on Thursday, August 15. The team defeated the “Saints & Sinners” team 4-3; and continued a tradition which dates to 1979. The coed softball league competed against four other teams this summer in 7-inning games. Other teams participating included Beach Bums, the Baja Bombers, and Game of Throws. The Wildwood Dads Club team also defeated slow-pitch softball foes from Havens and Beach at the end of the school year. The team added some moms to the diamond and became a summer league team. “The team started because (I think) many of us were super disappointed in our near decade losing streak,” said team manager Alex Shartsis. “We wanted a chance to win a game, so we signed up for the coed league.” Shartsis got the requisite signups and the rest is history. “In the winter of 2022-23,” explained Team Manager Adam Schwarz, “we played lots of ‘Eye of the Tiger,’ and recruited more talented and fun Wildwood parents and friends. We pirated a logo, ordered jerseys, destroyed a set of practice balls, and broke a window in Adam’s back yard.” Members of the WiId Things softball team: Abigail Johnson, Alex Shartsis, Brian Trowbridge, Cecilia Coronado Blake, Dirk Van Den Bos, Greg Wheeler, Jacqueline Perez Kalafate, Jennifer Gregovich, Matthew Deutsch, Megan Walsh, Mike Stearns, Morgan Driskill, Noah Schwartz, Roberto Kalafate, Steve Driskill

articles.text: Troop 1 inaugurated its first trip of the school year with a tubing trip at Caswell Memorial State Park in the Central Valley. The plan was to float for about a mile down the Stanislaus River, get out at a downstream beach and then walk a half mile back to do it all over again. Upon arrival, the Scouts couldn’t contain their excitement to wade or jump into the water. It was a great time with some Scouts preferring to just relax in their inner tubes and float down the river chatting with friends while others liked to be out and about, playing catch and swimming in the current. The water was crisp and refreshing with an occasional fallen tree or tree branch jutting out ominously from the river bed waiting to pop inner tubes of unsuspecting floaters. After spotting a lone cow by the riverbank, the Scouts stopped at a beach halfway through the trip to splash in the water. While many of the trees in the water posed hazards, one particular clump of trees and branches rose high out of the water, enabling the Scouts (and the scoutmaster) to climb up and jump several feet into the Keira Spina (left). Ben Callaway, Sawyer Heppner, Zeke Stein, Gabi Stein, Dylan Wallway, Theodore Cost, Zack Fisher, Kian Spina, Sammy Donnelly, Jack Chauncey, Finn Holder, Susannah Cantrill and Teo Wickner are excited to start floating. Troop 1 Scouts Samantha Pell, Susannah Cantrill, Moning Wang, Sasha Liu, and Julia Bencher enjoyed floating together. Troop 1 Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill leaps into the river while Susannah Cantrill and Kiera Spina wait to jump in. water – the highlight for many on the trip (see photo). After a second floating trip down the river, the Scouts changed out of their waterlogged clothing and set up their tents. Some Scouts cooked dinner, working to earn a Cooking merit badge, while others enjoyed a game of Three Flags Up with a frisbee. After a hearty dinner, the Scouts created a fire and roasted smores. As the night went on, the Scouts performed skits they had created such as “Crazy Uno.” To finish it off, one Scout relayed a classic Troop 1 story, “The Pink House”, to the new 6th graders participating in their first outing. Early the next morning after taking down camp, most Scouts embarked on a final float down the river while others waited at the downstream beach. The final trip down the river was just as good as the earlier floats, if not better. After reluctantly exiting the water, the Scouts formed a circle to discuss the trip highlights. All in all, it was a great introductory trip for Scouts new to Troop 1 and a fun new experience for the older Scouts. Theodore Cost is an 8th grader and a member of Piedmont Scouts Troop 1. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys water polo team, the defending North Coast Section champion, got its 2024 campaign underway on Friday and Saturday, August 30-31 at the Labor Day Bash tournament hosted by James Logan HS and Mission College in Fremont. They won two of four games, beating Marin Catholic 15-13 and losing 16-2 to James Logan on Friday, and beating Mission San Jose 12-7 and losing 12-8 to Alameda the following day. 12-7 win vs. Mission San Jose Piedmont got out to a 4-2 lead in the first quarter and went into halftime up 7-2. Both teams added a goal in the third quarter, 9-3, while PHS added three goals and conceded four in the final going. Final stats: Freshman Henry Stein led scoring with three goals, two assists, and a steal. Fellow freshman Rylan Patty had two goals, one assist, and three steals. Charlie Wright had two goals and an assist. Leo Hurwitz had a goal, two assists, and two steals. Elles Krieckhaus scored two goals. Yotam Kariv had one goal. 12-8 loss to Alameda Piedmont’s meeting with Alameda was a rematch of the D2 NCS Championship game, this time going in favor of the Hornets. Alameda led 5-2 by the end of the first quarter and 7-4 by halftime. Piedmont couldn’t cut away at the deficit in the third quarter, trailing 10-7 going into the fourth. PHS could only amass one goal in the final going, allowing two. Final stats: Krieckhaus had three goals, one assist, and one steal. Stein had two goals and an assist. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team opened its season on Friday, August 30 with a one-sided 46-14 loss to Salesian in its first game at Witter Field since 2022. After scoring the game’s opening score and clinging onto a 14-14 tie in the third quarter, the Highlanders gave up 32 unanswered points in the second half. “It was a tough game. articles.text: The Piedmont Highlanders JV football team started the 2024 season with a hard fought 14-14 tie against Salesian on Friday, August 30 at Witter Field. This year’s JV team is ripe with young talent, including 19 freshman pumped up to get experience on the gridiron. It was a memorable day for many, joining in on their very first High School football game. Piedmont’s returning sophomores Daniel King, Noah Hussain, Colby Hong, and Diego Hurwitz were named team captains by head coach Pouyan Assadi. PHS won the toss and decided to kick off to open the game. Salesian started on its own 37 yard line and drove all 63 yards for a touchdown in just two plays, including a 58-yard passing touchdown up the sideline. Salesian led 8-0 after a successful two-point conversion. But the Highlanders were ready to return the favor on Salesias when freshman quarterback Jimmy Lagios stepped to the line on their first play from scrimmage. With just enough blocking, Lagios tossed a perfect throw to Hurwitz, taking it 52 yards to the house for a touchdown. Piedmont trailed 8-6 after coming up short on a two-point conversion. The rest of the first quarter remained scoreless with both teams were playing good defense. It wasn’t until late in the second quarter when Salesian marched Photo by JC Curran Returning sophomores Diego Hurwitz (left), Daniel King, Noah Hussian, and Colby Hong were named captains ahead of JV football’s season-opener against Salesian. their way to the four-yard line on a multiple-play drive with broken tackles, punching it into the end zone with a little over three minutes left in the half. The Pride went into halftime holding a 14-6 lead. Salesian’s 14-6 lead remained through the third quarter with back-and-forth possessions and fumbles for both sides. In the fourth quarter, inside freshman linebacker George Saunders recovered his third fumble of the game to put Piedmont in a great position in the Pride’s red zone. Piedmont took advantage, scoring their second touchdown on a pass from Lagios to tight end George Saunders. Now trailing 14-12, PHS was forced to go for a two-point conversion. articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek will host a plein air workshop, where guests are invited to paint on garden grounds under the supervision of a local artist. Nancy Roberts, the Garden’s Artist in Residence this Fall will lead the outdoor workshop. A retired architect, she is a local professional artist, educator, arts community volunteer who exhibits her work in several Bay Area galleries. She organizes “paintouts” for the Contra Costa Plein Air group. Attendees will learn how to capture the shapes, colors and patterns on location with the versatile and expressive medium of acrylic paint. Roberts starts the workshop with a demonstration, then attendees will create their own painting with the instructors’ help and engagement. The workshop will be held on Wednesday, September 18, from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. Students are asked to bring their own portable easels and paint supplies. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ event/workshop-plein-air-in-thegarden/. Artist Nancy Roberts at work outside at Bancroft Gardens ®

articles.text: SF Opera in Golden Gate Park celebrates SF Opera’s 101st season San Francisco Opera’s famous free performance in Golden Gate Park is this Sunday, September 8, featuring stars from the company’s 2024–25 season. “Opera in the Park,” is now in its 48th year and is presented by the opera company and by the San Francisco Chronicle. The free concert celebrates the opening of the San Francisco Opera season, and traditionally draws thousands of attendees annually for a free afternoon of arias, duets and popular songs at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. Featured vocal soloists include sopranos Julie Adams, Aleksandra Kurzak and Olivia Smith; mezzo-sopranos Hyona Kim and Daniela Mack; tenors Roberto Alagna, Arturo Chacón-Cruz and Moisés Salazar; baritone Brian Mulligan; and bass-baritone Jongwon Han. Music Director Eun Sun Kim leads the performances, with Company General Director Matthew Shilvock serving as emcee. A rendition of the brindisi (drinking song) from Giuseppe Verdi’s La Traviata traditionally ends this time-honored Bay Area tradition. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets and their own food and beverages. Food trucks will also be onsite. The event is free and no tickets are required. Visit https://www. sfopera.com/seasons/opera-inthe-park/ to learn more. The event begins at 1:30 p.m.

articles.text: A tongue twisting dance tune from Brazil. A centuries old Korean folk song. An ode to pigeons from Zimbabwe. These were among the songs performed by World Harmony Chorus (WHC) at its most recent concert in June. All were sung in their original languages, in four-part harmony with no instrumentation sung by an enthusiastic, non-auditioned community chorus, many of whom were singing in a chorus for the first time. In the hands of any lesser director, this combination could be a recipe for disaster. But under Betsy Blakeslee’s masterful direction, a capacity audience at the Piedmont Center for the Arts thrilled to the diverse musical repertoire. The East Bay branch has been fortunate to have Betsy Blakeslee as its director for 16 years. World Harmony Chorus was founded in 1999 by Daniel Steinberg, who wanted to bring music-making into the lives of people who never thought they could sing. Twenty-five years later, WHC has branches in Palo Alto and Santa Cruz, directed by Steinberg, and in Berkeley, directed by Blakeslee. Steinberg arranges nearly all the music himself. Chorus members are sometimes bewildered at the beginning of the semester, but with patient teaching, over 100 amateur singers from around the Bay Area find joy in mastering the material and bringing the music to life. The fall semester starts Tuesday, October 1. The East Bay branch rehearses weekly on Tuesdays from 7:00-9:00 p.m. at the Berkeley Shambhala Meditation Center in in downtown Berkeley at 2288 Fulton Street. Arrive between 6:45-6:55 p.m. No auditions, no experience needed, no sight reading required. Musical adventures await for adults and children eight and above accompanied by a participating adult. pages.text: Wednesday, September 4, 2024 19 The Musical Gourmet Food for thought By Joseph Gold The inspiration came at the right time. It came in the person of a blonde Viking – perfect of form and personality, and a musical genius as well. This guy was generous, friendly and diplomatic, with perfectly timed humor. There was even a popular song about him - “Oleanna.” There were other popular musical super stars at the time. They played hundreds of concerts every year. Classical music was the thing that everyone wanted. But it was Ole Bull who became the most Americanized and did the most to bolster our national spirit. He gave the people what they wanted musically, and he The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet educated them at the same time. It was brilliant. This genius of the past is often ridiculed by the iconoclasts of today. Fortunately, a friend made an historical discovery which caused me to reevaluate some individuals, and Ole Bull is one of them. A Norwegian virtuoso violinist and composer (1810-1880), Bull did not have a huge repertoire as a violinist. He was happy to play the same pieces over and over again. The public didn’t mind, and they applauded vociferously. The thousands of dollars that he earned were given to charities around the world. What impresses me the most is that Ole Bull was one of the most deeply profound observers in the history of music. He was a violinist Sherlock Holmes. Every violinist would be advised to read his brilliant observations. Sadly, there is no recorded documentation of how he sounded. Generally speaking, artists of the past combined a brilliant technique with poetry to convey their art. Success today relies on speed, superficiality, and ridiculous stage deportment. I try to keep myself up-to-date musically. The pop music of the past was very interesting, and the artists of those days had very thorough musical training. Not so today. A musical example comes to mind. I was in a store the other day and listened to some music. The song was the usual type. As I listened, I noticed that the song had just one chord. It kept repeating over and over again… the same chord. Some people told me they like that song. Genius gives us food for thought. If we continue down the other road, we will have coprophagia. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, September 4, 2024 MOVIES FOR ADULTS By Chris Honoré Ready Player One, directed by Steven Spielberg, begs for exposition. In fact, it’s crammed full of stuff to comment on; the challenge is how to best sort it all out so that the commentary coheres on this one-dimensional page. First, the film is based on the best-selling Ernest Cline novel of the same title. Cline also partnered with Zak Penn to write the screenplay. Adapting Cline’s story for the screen, however, poses a problem because it is really two stories offered as one. Ready Player One (great title) opens with 18-year-old Wade Watts (Tye Sheridan) heading home. The year is 2045, the place is Columbus, Ohio, and Wade’s neighborhood is definitely not Spielberg’s archetypal burb, one with trimmed grass and affluent two-story houses. Housing is called “the stacks,” meaning towers of rusting RVs and mobile homes, placed precariously, one on top of the other. Wade lives in one and his hood looks like an overgrown junkyard, discarded detritus, and a warren of old cars and garbage. His reality is oppressive and seemingly hopeless. He is also without parents and living with a sketchy aunt and her boyfriend du jour. So it is no wonder that every chance Wade, who is part of what is referred to as the “missing milOlivia Cooke, Win Morisaki, Lena Waithe and Philip Zhao in Ready Player One Ready Player One lions,” literally and virtually goes missing into a reality known as the Oasis (Anthropocentric Sensory Immersive Simulation). It’s a virtual world of kaleidoscopic colors, avatars, a small cohort of friends, and a level of intensity that will likely never exist in his real dystopian world. The Oasis knows no limitations other than one’s imagination. It’s spectacular as well as a spectacle. And woven into the Oasis is an announced Easter Egg hunt, defined as three keys hidden by its late creator, James Haliday (Mark Rylance), somewhere in this virtual reality. The person/avatar who finds all three keys will inherit all the rights to the Oasis as well as Haliday’s half trillion-dollar fortune. Also in the hunt is Wade’s nemesis, Nolan Sorrento (Ben Mendelsohn), CEO of Innovative Online Industries, who wants ownership of the Oasis for commercial purposes. Its inherently positive construct is what attracts Wade, whose avatar is Parzival, the mythical seeker of the Holy Grail. So the race for the three keys is on. Most of the story will be spent in the Oasis with Parzival and a girl, Art3mis (Olivia Cooke), known in the real world as Samantha. Their interaction is far more compelling when it is set in the Oasis than those brief breaks back on the mean streets of the stacks. Or those moments spent with Wade in his narrow room when he’s hooked up to his virtual reality gear. Win Morisaki stars in Ready Player One Parzival, as we learn, is far more animated and cool than Wade, as portrayed by a somewhat flat Sheridan. Another example would be Art3mis, with her anomie eyes, lots of attitude, and spiky, multi-colored hair; she’s wonderful to watch and it’s clear why Parzival is attracted to her. Plus she fearlessly rides a very hot, red Shotaro Kaneda motorcycle. Parzival’s ride is a tricked out DeLorean, straight out of Back to the Future, the hit 80s blockbuster. Ready Player One is stuffed full of 80s pop culture artifacts and references. I found the Oasis and its multitude of characters appealing. The only downside was the writing. The plot, both virtual and real, was pretty thin, The narrative is held together by a series of vignettes: battles and races and chases all taking place for the most part in the Oasis. True, act three does take Wade/Parzival and Samantha/ Art3mis back to the real world for the finale (a prolonged chase) as well as the story’s denouement. It’s an uplifting ending; but the question is, will they stay there? Ready Player One. Directed by Steven Spielbrg. Starring Tye Sherman, Olivia Cooke, Ben Mendelsohn. 2 hrs., 20 min. Rated PG-13. And even then its audience may indeed be those who find pleasure in taking a deep dive into the extraordinary work that for decades has been the signature of Studio Ghibli from Japan. The hand-drawn animation of Pom Poka is remarkable, wrapped in wonderfully imagined moments. The weakness of the film resides not with its art but in the storytelling. First, you should know that the words Pom Poko refer to what are called, in Japanese mythology, tanuki, or “raccoon dogs”. They look like a cross between a raccoon and a wolverine. They are thought to be as amiable as a hedgehog. These raccoons are said to be mischievous and capable of using the “illusion science” of shape-shifting in which they can transform themselves into anthropomorphic animals. The story begins in 1960 when the habitat of the tanuki on the outskirts of Tokyo is threatened by a giant subdivision, called Tama Hills, causing distress for not only the forest wildlife, but most especially the tanuki. The story resumes in 1990 when the tanuki matriarch, Oroku (Tess MacNeille), plus the warlike chief, Gonta (Clancy Brown), and the resourceful Shoukichi (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) urge the tribe to resist the expanding encroachment. And so begins the confrontation between the tanuki and the developers, realistic and cartoonish, occasionally spiced up with trickery, as when some tanuki go undercover, shape-shifting to appear human while roaming the urban streets. The threads that stich the narrative together, both melodramatic and cartoonish, are numerous, but often lack focus. At one point, a pageant of mystical creatures are on parade, as well as a huge tsunami, both intended to scare the construction crews and the townies. This tanuki strategy also includes construction-site sabotage that does frighten and kills some of the workers. Much of Pom Poko is surreal, at times manic, relying on the sustained attempt by the tanuki to terrorize the humans. It’s a spectacle leading to a dour denouement which sums up what proves to be a not-family friendly fable. Pom Poko. Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahata. With the voices of Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Clancy Brown, Tess MacNeille and Andre Stojka. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG. Released in 1994, Now streaming on prime/ MAX/apple tv/Fandango.

articles.text: A slice of a freshly baked Summer Fruits Cake Photos by Deborah Quok As summer wanes, so do my favorite summer fruit crops of peaches, nectarines and plums. This cake, which is pretty forgiving when it comes to making substitutions, is a brilliant showcase for perfectly ripe stone fruits. I appreciate the versatility of this cake: it can be dressed up for fancy presentation, or served simply to allow the fragrant fruit and tender cake to make a statement on their own. The other bonus for making this now is that many of these fruits are at seasonal low pricing from your local farmers markets. articles.text: Remakes of old movies can be disappointing, but sometimes they’re terrific. Take the great comedy classic, Some Like It Hot, for example, which is a retooling of a 1930s German musical. Another irresistible remake is 1996’s The Birdcage, an American take on the French comedy hit, La Cage au Folles. No one is disappointed by the American version – they’re laughing too hard, and locals will get a chance to laugh, too, when the film is shown at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at the next Flix Fest. Directed by Mike Nichols from a screenplay by Elaine May (remember Nichols and May?), The Birdcage won a Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by a Cast. It stars Robin Williams and Nathan Lane as a gay couple whose son arrives at their Miami nightclub with the surprise announcement that he plans to marry soon. The problem is that his fiancee’s parents are an ultraconservative couple, deftly played by Gene Hackman and Diane Wiest. (If you’ve ever wanted to see Gene Hackman in drag, here’s your chance.) The Birdcage was released on March 8, 1996, to positive reviews and significant commercial success. It debuted at the top of the North American box office and stayed there for the following three weeks, grossing $185.3 million on a $31 million budget. It’s seen as groundbreaking, because it was one of few films from a major studio to feature LGBTQ characters at its center. The Birdcage will be screened on Thursday, September 12, at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the Rec. Dept. can be done at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. Piedmont Flix Fest movies are scheduled on the second Thursday of each month and are free. The next movie is the 2003 German comedy, Schultze Gets the Blues, to be shown on October 10.

articles.text: A new class at Piedmont Adult School, “Building Skills for Successful Family Research,” aims at helping aspiring family historians who want to learn about the lives of their ancestors. The class will focus on teaching foundational skills to identify relevant records and where to find them, documenting sources, and assessing record reliability. The course will consist of six classes plus optional field trips to the Oakland Family Search Library and the California Genealogical Society Library. The class will be taught by Pam Brett, who has been researching her own family history for the last 25 years. She has taught numerous classes for the California Genealogical Society and has traveled extensively to attend genealogical conferences and workshops and to conduct on-site research. “Many people have dabbled in genealogy,” says Brett, “but they often hit a brick wall or lose interest when results are slim. This class goes far beyond what you can accomplish on a genealogy website. Students will learn how to dig deep and uncover the inforInstructor Pam Brett’s ancestors came to America in colonial times and moved often, leading her toward research in 29 states and the District of Columbia. mation that really makes family histories come alive.” Are you interested in researching your family history, but not sure how to get started? Have you tried some genealogy websites, with unsatisfying results? Do you want to get off your computer and into the fascinating world of libraries, courthouses, archives and town halls? articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group tries to get to every safe walking Piedmont street during the year, but they hadn’t been to some of the streets west and north of Dracena Park. This part of Piedmont, like a lot of Piedmont, was developed after the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake through the 1920s. The walkers thought it would be fun to see the streets and consider some of the homes on them. Zillow research of a random set provided when they were built, their sizes, and estimated selling prices. With information shared about the other homes, the walkers could have fun guessing its listing price. However, before the group started walking some background information was shared. In 2020, Piedmont’s population was 11,270 with 3,924 housing units according to Wikipedia. The median price of homes sold in the last 12 months was $2,550,000. The walkers went across Carmel Avenue to Blair and Ricardo Avenues for their first selected house to consider. Architect Jim Kellogg called it a “bungalow beauty,” a 3 bedroom/3 bath built in 1907 with an estimated value of $2.4 million. The next Ricardo house up the street (by coincidence) was Sharona and Jack Fischrup’s original clapboard brick exterior home of 33 years. Then it was over to Arroyo Avenue to York Drive and a 5 bedroom/3 bath house built in 1959 on rightof-way land made available when the Key System trains stopped running. Further up York was a 1922, 5 bedroom/7 bath being completely remodeled. The walkers went down Cambridge Way to Manor Drive for their last home before the actual “for sale” home and their guessing. This last one was built in 1915, has 3 bedrooms and 3.5 baths, and is worth 3 million according to Zillow. Finally they came to the house with a For Sale sign in the front yard. It is a Tudor style house with 2,521 square feet and was built in 1921. All the walkers fell for the flowery language and guessed more than the listing price of $2.295 million. Thankfully, no one had brought a checkbook. It was all in fun, but it was time for the walkers to make their return to the Exedra. They went back via Holly Place, a hidden 272-foot path from York to Ricardo, and then had a delightful walk through Dracena Park to Park Way, Hillside and Magnolia Avenues. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. A record 49 walkers and three K-9 best friends showed up for the last Wednesday Walk of the summer on August 28. Among those participating were Sharona and Jack Fischrup, Denny McGee, Karin Fetherston, Charlene Louie, Nancy Henn, Mari Negron with K-9 best friend Dakota, Lisa Euphrat, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kuo, Peggy Shultz, Adrienne Hamlin, Martin Levy, Judy Sokoloff, Claudine Bach, Linda Peacock, Elizabeth Richter, Pat Keller, Dottie Hutch, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Nancy Olsen, Lois Price, Meghan Bennett, Larry Olsen, Mark Frost, Rick Eigenbrode, Pat Nicholas, Gloria DaSilva, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Angela Tom, Robert Lang, Gary Rogers, Melba Yee, Kat Lang, Garrett Clifford, Matt Gerhardt, Ken Hubbert, Brenda Ferrero, Chuck Oraftik, Greg Keller, Bill Ahern, Irene Thompson, Lori Rubens, Patsy Forsyth and Dick Carter. The group was pleased Eric Behrens brought his sister, Yvonne Behrens, who was visiting from Virginia.

articles.text: Dear Abby: What’s this doggy yap about a Pawsome Day for Dogs at the Giants? I’ve heard that I’ll get a free leash with the Giants logo if my parents take me. Is that fur real? And when is it? –Jennifer and Charlie the Frenchie Dear Jennifer and Charlie: Yes, It’s true. This year the Giants are hosting two Dog Days. The second one is on Saturday, September 28th at 1:05 against the feathery Cardinals. Come early and walk in the pawsome pre-game parade on the field. All furry costumes are welcome and some of the proceeds from your ticket purchase will benefit the SF SPCA. When you’re done barking, take a seat and cheer the Giants onto victory as they take on St. Louis. All dogs are welcome. If you get hungry your mom can always buy you a hot dog and you’ll receive a lovely orange Giants leash to show off to all your canine friends. Learn more at Dog Days at sfgiants.com. It’ll be a doggone good time. Lots of sniffs and howls. Go Giants! –Abby Dear Abby: I’ve seen a lot of mobile groomers in Piedmont. Do you have any opinions? It seems like a nice option for my Ulti-Mutt, but am I barking up the wrong tree? Woof. –Thug the Pug and Dad Dear Thug and Dad: I haven’t used any of the mobile groomers. I’ve seen a Groom Buggy van around town and Tiffany’s Mobile Grooming van too. When I’ve asked owners, they seem to be pleased with the results. We use a groomer near Park Boulevard. It used to be called Poodles ala Pamela and is now Elegant Grooming at 1310 Glenfield Avenue (Oakland 92602, tel. 510-612-5027). We have had excellent results, with fragrant fur as well as a very happy, clean dog. Drive to Park Blvd. and park near Marzano Restaurant. Our experience has always been great, the groomers are kind and it’s reasonably priced. We’ve had good luck, and grooming is good for the soul. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.

articles.text: Troop 11 Scouts just backpacked 35 miles through the Grand Canyon of the Tuolumne in Yosemite. On the first day, the backpackers began by descending 3,000 feet down the steep walls of the valley over the course of 12 slightly smoky miles. At the bottom, Scouts were met with their first view of the Tuolumne River and immediately everyone jumped in the water to cool off and to relieve their aching muscles. The next day, the group had a late start at 11 a.m. The Scouts hiked alongside the river where gorgeous pools and beautiful views of cliffs could be seen. After lunch, the crew decided to push on for a 1200-foot climb. It was well worth the effort because there were 40-foot waterfalls from a creek to swim under and incredible views of the canyon at the top. On the way up, Scouts Top row: Elles Kreickhaus (left), George Stein, Henry Stein, Sean McKee, Drew Kobal, Jack Shim, Oliver Amen, Colin Amen, Ted Eisemon, Justin Amen. Bottom row: Julie Stein (left), Rob Amen, Laura Amen, Jason Stein, Eric Eisemon Scouts carry all their gear for 35 miles. Playing in water slides Drew Kobal at LeConte falls spotted their first rattlesnakes of the trip. The hike on Thursday totaled eight miles and 1,500 feet of elevation. At the end of day, everyone was delighted to find a lovely campsite with what one Scout described as “some of the best natural water slides I’ve ever been on.” Slippery granite slabs sloping into a deep pool of water were the perfect combination for epic slides down the rocks. After a dinner of freeze dried food, the Scouts fell asleep under an unparalleled view of the stars and frequent meteors shooting by. Friday also included some epic scenery. Starting out it felt like hiking ln the middle of a desert, but it soon changed into a bug-infested rain forest. The crew escaped by hiking up a completely barren granite rock face, and then climbing under boulders the size of houses. Lunch was the pinnacle of the day. The Scouts found a perfect place to eat after their enormous climb. The spot was a wide section of the river that led into an incredible waterfall that cascaded down the same cliffs the crew had just hiked. But the climb was not over. Another 1000 feet had to be ascended before the group could pitch a campsite. The work did not go unrewarded. Incredible Troop 11 Scouts hike alongside the river. Swimming in a waterfall at a creek

articles.text: In recent years, KCOM’s coverage has largely been recordings of public meetings. The road to reviving and expanding KCOM has been a long one. In the past, city staff have had to deal with aged equipment which has required extensive maintenance and troubleshooting. Additionally, the City has hired two new broadcast technicians, Richard Daniels and Dreu Towan, to assist with regular broadcasting by the station.
